q: What limitations or open problems do the authors acknowledge?
text:
The authors acknowledge these limitations and open problems:

No explicit pg. The generator defines its distribution only implicitly, so there is no direct way to evaluate p(x) p. 7. Table 2 lists it as "not explicitly represented, may be approximated with Parzen density estimation" p. 7.

Synchronizing D and G. G must not be trained too much without updating D, or it collapses many values of z onto the same x, the "Helvetica scenario," which destroys the diversity needed to model pdata p. 7. They compare this to keeping the negative chains of a Boltzmann machine up to date p. 7.

Weak evaluation. Parzen window estimates have high variance and do not work well in high dimensions, and the authors say generative models that can sample but not estimate likelihood call for further research on how to evaluate them p. 6.

Theory versus practice. The proofs are nonparametric, but in practice they optimize θg rather than pg, and using a multilayer perceptron introduces multiple critical points, leaving it without theoretical guarantees p. 5.

Training cost. They list better ways of coordinating G and D, or better distributions to sample z from, as a way to accelerate training p. 8. Early in training, log(1 − D(G(z))) can also saturate, so they suggest maximizing log D(G(z)) instead p. 3.

q: How does the theory in section 4 differ from what they actually trained in section 5?
text:
Section 4 works in a nonparametric setting, while section 5 trains finite networks, and the gaps show up in four places.

First, what is being optimized. The proofs treat pg as a free distribution, studying convergence "in the space of probability density functions" p. 3. In practice the authors optimize θg of a generator G(z; θg), which represents only a limited family of distributions p. 5.

Second, the discriminator. Proposition 2 assumes G and D have enough capacity and that D reaches its optimum given G at every step p. 5. Algorithm 1 instead alternates k steps of D with one of G, and the experiments used k = 1, the cheapest option p. 4. The authors note that full optimization of D in the inner loop is computationally prohibitive and would overfit finite datasets p. 3.

Third, the generator objective. The theory analyzes minimizing log(1 − D(G(z))) p. 3. The paper suggests maximizing log D(G(z)) instead, because it gives stronger gradients early in training while sharing the same fixed point p. 3. The text does not say which of the two was used in the experiments, though Algorithm 1 is written with the minimizing form p. 4.

Fourth, convexity. The convergence argument relies on convexity in pg, but an MLP generator introduces multiple critical points in parameter space, so the authors admit it lacks theoretical guarantees p. 5.

Also, the evaluation in section 5 is a Parzen window estimate fitted to samples, not a measurement of how close pg is to pdata p. 6.

q: Which results in Table 1 support the paper's claims, and how strong is that evidence?
text:
Table 1 gives Parzen window log-likelihood estimates on MNIST and TFD, and the bolded entries are 225 ± 2 for adversarial nets on MNIST, 2110 ± 50 for Stacked CAE on TFD, and 2057 ± 26 for adversarial nets on TFD p. 6.

What supports the paper: on MNIST, adversarial nets (225 ± 2) beat Deep GSN (214 ± 1.1), DBN (138 ± 2) and Stacked CAE (121 ± 1.6), and the gaps exceed the reported standard errors. On TFD, they beat DBN (1909 ± 66) and Deep GSN (1890 ± 29), though the 2057 versus 2110 gap to Stacked CAE is within roughly one combined standard error, so those two are not clearly separated.

How strong this is: modest. The authors themselves say this likelihood estimate has high variance and performs poorly in high dimensions, though it is the best method they know of p. 6. The MNIST standard error is computed across test examples, while the TFD one is computed across folds, so the error bars are not like for like p. 6. The MNIST comparison is against models on the real-valued version of the dataset p. 6.

The table also says nothing about the theory in section 4, such as convergence to pdata. The authors claim only that their samples are competitive, not better p. 6. The table fits that modest claim and does not go beyond it.
